questions.title: Shared strategy
questions.text: Your managers know how to translate the company’s strategy into concrete actions for their teams.
questions.anchor_low: No one knows where the company is headed
questions.anchor_high: Each manager knows how to translate it into priorities for their team

kpis.name: % of managers who understand the strategy
kpis.desc: Measures how well the company’s strategy is truly understood by managers. Low understanding = misaligned execution.

kpis.name: % aligned initiatives
kpis.desc: Verify that ongoing initiatives are consistent with the declared strategic direction.

kpis.name: Formalized and up-to-date strategic document
kpis.desc: Presence and updating of a formal document defining the strategy. Absence = implicit and unshared strategy.

kpis.name: Number of active simultaneous strategic priorities
kpis.desc: Too many simultaneous priorities can分散资源和注意力。最佳：最多3-5个同时活跃的优先级。

kpis.name: Strategy review frequency
kpis.desc: Frequency with which the strategy is reviewed and updated. Too infrequent = outdated strategy.

actions_preview.name: Strategy cascade workshop
actions_preview.desc: Conduct structured sessions (max 8 people) to translate the strategy into functional operational objectives, with comprehension verification through facilitated Q&A.

actions_preview.name: Individual strategy scorecard
actions_preview.desc: Define a personal scorecard for each manager that links function KPIs to strategic goals, with quarterly review.

actions_preview.name: Recurring executive briefing
actions_preview.desc: Establish a monthly 60-minute briefing with the AD to update managers on strategy status and gather operational feedback.

actions_preview.name: Strategic portfolio review
actions_preview.desc: Map all active initiatives onto a strategic impact / effort matrix, archiving misaligned ones and redefining priorities.

actions_preview.name: Entry initiative filter
actions_preview.desc: Implement a formal process (minimum business case) for the approval of new initiatives, with an obligatory strategic alignment criterion.

actions_preview.name: Quarterly alignment check-in
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a quarterly portfolio review with explicit questions: 'Is this initiative still strategically relevant?'

actions_preview.name: Strategic document drafting
actions_preview.desc: Facilitate the creation of a structured strategic document (maximum 10 pages) including vision, priorities, three-year objectives, and reference KPIs.

actions_preview.name: Annual update process
actions_preview.desc: Define a fixed annual review calendar for the strategic document, with designated owners and formal approval from the CDO or AD.

actions_preview.name: Distribution and onboarding
actions_preview.desc: Structure a distribution and presentation process of the document to all managers, including documented Q&A sessions.

actions_preview.name: Strategic prioritization workshop
actions_preview.desc: Facilitate a prioritization session with top management using the impact/probability matrix to reduce priorities to a maximum of 5.

actions_preview.name: Moratorium on new initiatives
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a formal mechanism for a temporary stop to the start-up of new initiatives until ongoing projects reach defined milestones.

actions_preview.name: Project killing criteria
actions_preview.desc: Define explicit criteria for suspending or closing non-strategic initiatives with a bi-annual review.

actions_preview.name: Annual strategic calendar
actions_preview.desc: Define and block in the corporate calendar annual strategy review sessions: 1 extended annually + 2 semi-annual reviews.

actions_preview.name: Market signal dashboard
actions_preview.desc: Implement a simple system (even just a monthly report) for monitoring key market signals relevant to the strategy.

actions_preview.name: Trigger-based review process
actions_preview.desc: Define trigger events (e.g., loss of key customer, regulatory change, new competitor) that automatically activate an extraordinary review.

blocks.text: When I first enter an Italian SME for the first time, the pattern that emerges is almost always the same. The founder has clear ideas about where they want to take the company. The leadership team partially knows these plans but often does not fully share them and rarely speaks openly about it. Employees know little or nothing about this and do not understand the rationale behind decisions affecting them.

It is not your problem, and it is measurable. According to a 2025 survey of over 3,500 workers, only one in three employees believes that senior management would openly and transparently answer questions about strategy and company finances. When asked the same question at the top levels, 56% agree. The gap between these two numbers is precisely where misunderstandings arise: those above think they have communicated, while those below are unaware.

The underlying cause, however, is cultural. I have seen many times founders and leaders keep the strategy close to their chest for a specific belief: that people would not understand it or worse, use it against the company. The logic of 'better not say too much' trickles down to operational levels, creating an organization that moves in fits and starts, with silos that do not communicate.

The company is an organism whose parts must think as one to achieve challenging goals. Keeping people in the dark does not make them more controllable; it fosters distrust, suspicion, and disengagement. A vicious cycle ensues: the founder lacks trust, employees feel uninvolved, no one rows in the same direction, and the founder confirms that they could not rely on them.

The cost is real and hardest to see on the balance sheet: projects that start but do not finish, initiatives that overlap, talented people leaving because they do not understand where they are going. In the mandates I have followed, the gap between what senior management decided and what the organization was actually doing was almost always larger than what senior management imagined.

The reframing is this: strategy is not a secret to protect but a compass that becomes powerful only when many use it. It does not mean everyone must know everything; it means they must have enough knowledge to decide, every morning, in which direction to move. Without that 'enough,' the strategy remains a document no one uses.

references: SurveyMonkey, "2025 Workplace Culture and Trends," August 2025 - 3,573 full-time U.S. workers surveyed from July 25 to August 3, 2025, with an estimated margin of error of +/- 2.0 percentage points, weighted data based on the American Community Survey. https://www.surveymonkey.com/curiosity/surveymonkey-research-workplace-culture-and-trends/

questions.title: Defining objectives
questions.text: Each business objective has a number that measures it, a deadline, and a responsible person with a name and surname.
questions.anchor_low: Vague objectives, no one is accountable
questions.anchor_high: A measurable target, deadline, and responsible person for each

kpis.name: % of objectives defined with KPIs (SMART)
kpis.desc: Percentage of objectives defined with SMART criteria: specific, measurable, with a deadline and a responsible person.

kpis.name: % of objectives assigned with explicit responsibility
kpis.desc: Each objective must have an explicitly defined responsible party. Without ownership, there is no accountability.

kpis.name: % alignment of individual and corporate objectives
kpis.desc: Degree of coherence between employees' personal goals and the company's overall goals. Misalignment = demotivation.

kpis.name: Average number of KPIs per function/team
kpis.desc: Too many KPIs for a function can disperse focus. The optimal number is 3-5 per team.

kpis.name: Active structured performance management system
kpis.desc: Indicates whether there exists a structured system to monitor and evaluate performance. Absence = subjective evaluation.

actions_preview.name: OKR / SMART workshop
actions_preview.desc: Train the management on the SMART/OKR methodology and facilitate the rewriting of existing objectives into measurable ones.

actions_preview.name: Standardized objective template
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a mandatory standardized template for defining objectives, including fields for KPI reference, baseline, and target.

actions_preview.name: Annual goal review
actions_preview.desc: Establish a formal process of validating goals at the beginning of the year with facilitated SMART checks by a consultant.

actions_preview.name: Objective-owner matrix
actions_preview.desc: Create and maintain an up-to-date matrix that associates each strategic objective to a single named owner.

actions_preview.name: Objective acceptance signature
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a formal process of goal acceptance by managers, with signed documents stored in HR.

actions_preview.name: Semestral accountability review
actions_preview.desc: Conduct a semestral review with each manager to verify the status of objectives and update ownership.

actions_preview.name: Objective cascading
actions_preview.desc: Facilitate a top-down cascading process: from the company's strategic objectives to functional objectives, down to individual goals.

actions_preview.name: Alignment visualization map
actions_preview.desc: Create a shared visual representation of the goal tree (strategy map) for all managers.

actions_preview.name: MBO alignment check
actions_preview.desc: Integrate an explicit moment for vertical goals alignment review into the existing MBO cycle.

actions_preview.name: KPI rationalization
actions_preview.desc: Reduce the number of KPIs per function to a maximum of 5-7 key ones through a facilitated prioritization session with responsible parties.

actions_preview.name: KPI hierarchy (leading/lagging)
actions_preview.desc: Structure KPIs into two levels: result-oriented KPIs (lagging) and process-oriented KPIs (leading), eliminating redundant ones.

actions_preview.name: KPI owner and frequency
actions_preview.desc: Assign an owner and update frequency to each KPI, removing those that are not regularly updated.

actions_preview.name: Performance Management System Design
actions_preview.desc: Designing a simple performance management system: goals + KPIs + periodic reviews + feedback, calibrated to the company size.

actions_preview.name: Pilot Implementation
actions_preview.desc: Implement the system on a pilot function for six months, gather feedback and optimize before full-scale rollout.

actions_preview.name: HR and Manager Training
actions_preview.desc: Train HR and managers on using the system, with a focus on conducting performance interviews.

blocks.text: At the start of each meeting, I always ask the same question: what is our goal for this year? The answers almost always fall into the same category. Grow, improve service, become more market present. They are intentions, not goals: none of those sentences tells an employee what they need to do on Monday morning.
The missing step is always the same: the number. Without a measure, a goal cannot be achieved or missed, and at year-end, the review becomes a discussion about interpretations.

There is also a resistance I have learned to recognize: writing down a number means exposing oneself. As long as the goal remains vague, no one can be held responsible for not achieving it. It’s a form of protection, and like all protections, it has a cost: it removes the company’s ability to correct course before it is too late.
A goal is not what I want to achieve; it is what I am willing to measure. If it does not have a number associated with it, it is not a goal, but a hope. And hopes are not manageable.

The second step is the name. A goal assigned to a function is not assigned to anyone: functions do not decide; people do. When I ask who is responsible for a certain result and am told 'the sales team,' I already know that result will not be achieved.

The third thing is the deadline, which serves less as a control than one might think: it serves to protect. A date tells those working on something when they can consider themselves done. Without it, work never ends, and people burn out.

questions.title: Data-driven decisions
questions.text: Important decisions rest on figures as much as on the judgement of the people taking them.
questions.anchor_high: No big decision without the numbers in front of us

kpis.name: % of decisions supported by KPIs or data analysis
kpis.desc: Percentage of decisions based on data analysis or KPIs rather than on perception.

kpis.name: % of reports actually used
kpis.desc: Percentage of the reports produced that are actually read and used. High output with low readership is waste.

kpis.name: Level of trust in business data (survey)
kpis.desc: How far managers trust the accuracy and reliability of company data.

kpis.name: Average time to retrieve data for a decision
kpis.desc: Time required to find and open the data a decision needs. Slow data means slow decisions.

kpis.name: Number of data sources for strategic decisions
kpis.desc: How many independent sources contribute to an important decision. Three converging sources make a decision solid, one makes it fragile.

actions_preview.name: Data-driven decision protocol
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a simple rule whereby every proposal brought to a meeting carries at least one supporting figure with its source cited.

actions_preview.name: Pre-meeting dashboard
actions_preview.desc: Circulate a short report with the relevant KPIs before each board meeting, covering the items on the agenda.

actions_preview.name: Individual data literacy coaching
actions_preview.desc: Coach managers who are less comfortable with data one to one, so that both confidence and habit build up.

actions_preview.name: Report usage audit
actions_preview.desc: Ask the people who receive the reports which ones they actually read and which ones they ignore.

actions_preview.name: Report rationalization
actions_preview.desc: Remove or consolidate unused reports, reducing production burden and enhancing the quality of key reports.

actions_preview.name: Reporting feedback loop
actions_preview.desc: Establish a periodic mechanism for feedback from recipients to continuously improve the relevance of reports.

actions_preview.name: Data quality assessment
actions_preview.desc: Conduct a data quality assessment in primary sources (ERP, CRM, Excel sheets) identifying critical areas.

actions_preview.name: Data quality owner
actions_preview.desc: Nominate a data quality owner for each main data source responsible for quality and updating.

actions_preview.name: Data cleansing plan
actions_preview.desc: Define and implement a prioritised plan to cleanse the most critical data for management decisions.

actions_preview.name: Business data catalogue
actions_preview.desc: Create a simple data source catalogue indicating where to find each type of data and who to contact.

actions_preview.name: Self-service reporting
actions_preview.desc: Implement a self-service reporting tool (even as simple as Power BI or Metabase) to reduce requests to IT.

actions_preview.name: Pre-processed key data
actions_preview.desc: Pre-process the most requested data into standard reports available on-demand, reducing preparation time.

actions_preview.name: Data source mapping
actions_preview.desc: Census of all data sources used by management in decision-making, identifying redundancies and gaps.

actions_preview.name: Prioritised data source integration
actions_preview.desc: Integrate the 3-5 most critical data sources into a single consolidated view, eliminating the need for manual aggregation.

actions_preview.name: Data source governance
actions_preview.desc: Define which sources are 'official' for each type of decision, reducing the proliferation of alternative sources.

blocks.text: I have sat in plenty of meetings where the same question got three different answers depending on who opened the file. This was not because anyone was lying, it was because each person was looking at a different extract, updated at a different moment.

Over two years, the share of Italian SMEs analysing their own data has risen from 26.6% to 42.7%. The figure is growing quickly, yet the gap remains wide, since micro and small businesses stand at 41.9% against 83.6% for large companies. Companies with the right tools decide on the basis of data, while the others are still deciding in the dark.

What I see is that the problem rarely lies in the lack of data. The data exist, but reaching them takes time, so when a decision has to be taken quickly it gets taken without it. The real measure is how fast you can get your hands on the data you already have.
Deciding on the basis of data still leaves room for judgement, with the difference that the judgement now starts from one shared baseline instead of three separate ones.

I have seen companies build beautiful dashboards that no one uses, and others decide well on three numbers written by hand on a whiteboard. The difference lies in the fact that everyone in the second company shares those three numbers and nobody disputes them.
Before you buy an analytics tool, work out which five numbers your company actually decides on. If you can’t list them, no dashboard will help because you won’t know what to put into it.

references: Istat, "Firms and ICT, 2025", Statistical Report, 15 December 2025. https://www.istat.it

questions.title: Operational Processes
questions.text: Key processes always run the same way, regardless of who executes them.
questions.anchor_low: Each one does it their own way
questions.anchor_high: Same process for everyone, every time

kpis.name: % processes documented and formalized
kpis.desc: Percentage of business processes that are documented, standardized, and formalized.

kpis.name: Average execution time of key processes
kpis.desc: Average time required to complete key operational processes from start to finish.

kpis.name: % processes with owner defined
kpis.desc: Percentage of processes with a defined owner. Processes without an owner are not improved.

kpis.name: % standardised processes vs variable processes
kpis.desc: Percentage of processes executed consistently in the same way, compared to those that vary by operator.

kpis.name: Average number of steps per process
kpis.desc: Number of average steps required to complete a process. More steps = greater complexity and risk of error.

kpis.name: Process variability rate (std dev times)
kpis.desc: Variability in the execution times of processes. High variability = process not under control.

actions_preview.name: Key process census
actions_preview.desc: Identify and census the 20-30 most critical business processes, defining the scope of priority documentation.

actions_preview.name: As-is process documentation
actions_preview.desc: Facilitate process mapping sessions with operational teams to document key processes in their current form (as-is).

actions_preview.name: Document repository
actions_preview.desc: Implement a centralized repository (e.g., SharePoint or Notion) for managing and updating process documentation.

actions_preview.name: Process time analysis
actions_preview.desc: Measure the actual execution times of the 5 identified key processes, identifying the slower phases.

actions_preview.name: Bottleneck identification
actions_preview.desc: Analyse the causes of slowdowns (approvals, delays, rework) and define prioritised corrective actions.

actions_preview.name: Optimization quick wins
actions_preview.desc: Implement minor effort optimizations (e.g., eliminating redundant steps, automating notifications) with immediate impact on timelines.

actions_preview.name: Process owner assignment
actions_preview.desc: Formally assign a process owner to each documented process with explicit responsibilities for performance and updates.

actions_preview.name: Process owner charter
actions_preview.desc: Define the mandate for each process owner: what they measure, how frequently, and what decisions they can make autonomously.

actions_preview.name: Process owner community
actions_preview.desc: Establish quarterly meetings among process owners to share best practices and common issues.

actions_preview.name: Identification of critical variability
actions_preview.desc: Identify processes with the highest variability, evaluate whether it is pathological (errors, lack of standards) or physiological (required personalization).

actions_preview.name: Standard operating procedures
actions_preview.desc: Define SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) for high-pathological variability processes and provide team training.

actions_preview.name: Conformity Monitoring
actions_preview.desc: Implement periodic compliance checks with immediate feedback to operators against standard procedures.

actions_preview.name: Value Stream Mapping
actions_preview.desc: Map the value stream of each key process by identifying steps that do not add value to internal/external customers.

actions_preview.name: Eliminate Redundant Steps
actions_preview.desc: Remove or consolidate unnecessary steps identified in Value Stream Mapping, simplifying operational workflows.

actions_preview.name: Lean Process Redesign
actions_preview.desc: Redesign more complex processes by applying lean principles with the objective of reducing the number of steps by 20-30%.

actions_preview.name: Basic Statistical Process Control
actions_preview.desc: Introduce systematic process time measurements to identify real variability and its causes.

actions_preview.name: Root cause of variability
actions_preview.desc: Analyse the causes of variability (variable input quality, differing competencies, unhandled exceptions) and define corrective actions.

actions_preview.name: Standardization of process inputs
actions_preview.desc: Standardize the most variable process inputs (templates, checklists, required data) to reduce variability at the source.

blocks.text: There's a signal I recognize immediately: when I ask how a process works and they respond with a person’s name. 'That’s Anna.' It’s not an answer about the process; it’s an answer about risk.

In rapidly growing companies, processes were not designed but evolved over time. Each individual found their own way of making things work, and that worked for years. The problem arises when the company doubles in size or when Anna retires.

Management, which should be the backbone of processes, is used by only 48.8% of Italian SMEs compared to 85.9% of large enterprises. Even where it exists, I have almost always found it supplemented by a parallel spreadsheet: those are the real processes.
Standardization does not mean rigidity. It means that the outcome is independent of who performs it.

The useful question is not 'do we have written procedures.' It's 'if a new person joins tomorrow, how long will they work like everyone else?' The time to get that answer is the measure of the process.

There’s then a benefit almost no one considers: a standardized process is the only thing that can be automated. Until each does it their own way, there's nothing to automate; there's just order to impose.

references: Istat, "Firms and ICT, 2025", Statistical Report, 15 December 2025. https://www.istat.it

questions.title: Project execution
questions.text: Projects are delivered on time and within the budget agreed at the start.
questions.anchor_low: Almost always late or over budget

kpis.name: % of projects completed on schedule
kpis.desc: Percentage of projects delivered by the originally planned date.

kpis.name: % of projects completed within budget
kpis.desc: Percentage of projects completed without exceeding the approved budget.

kpis.name: Schedule variance (average time deviation)
kpis.desc: Average deviation between planned and actual project completion dates.

kpis.name: Cost variance (average financial deviation)
kpis.desc: Average deviation between planned and actual project costs.

kpis.name: % of projects with objectives modified during execution
kpis.desc: Percentage of projects in which original objectives were modified during execution.

kpis.name: Average project start-up time (idea → start)
kpis.desc: Time that passes from the approval of a project to the actual operational launch of activities.

kpis.name: Time-to-market (decision → first measurable operational result)
kpis.desc: Time from the decision to initiate an initiative to the first measurable operational outcome. Measures end-to-end execution speed.

actions_preview.name: Analysis of historical delays
actions_preview.desc: Analyse projects from the last 2 years and identify systematic causes of delay (scope creep, resources, dependencies).

actions_preview.name: Milestone-based planning
actions_preview.desc: Review the project planning methodology by introducing intermediate verifiable milestones every 2-4 weeks.

actions_preview.name: Buffer management
actions_preview.desc: Introduce explicit buffers in project plans and establish a standard for managing them (Critical Chain Project Management).

actions_preview.name: Simplified Earned Value Management
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a simple cost tracking system for actuals vs. budget at each milestone, with automatic alerts.

actions_preview.name: Variance Governance
actions_preview.desc: Define variance thresholds beyond which formal escalation to the project sponsor is mandatory.

actions_preview.name: Bottom-up Cost Estimation
actions_preview.desc: Improve initial cost estimates through bottom-up methodologies and historical data from previous initiatives.

actions_preview.name: Structured Weekly Status Update
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a 15-minute structured weekly project status update: completed, planned, blocks.

actions_preview.name: Bi-weekly Gantt Review
actions_preview.desc: Review the project Gantt chart bi-weekly, updating remaining estimates based on actual status.

actions_preview.name: Mandatory recovery plan
actions_preview.desc: Implement a formal recovery plan when schedule variance exceeds 10%.

actions_preview.name: Monthly budget tracking
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a monthly cost tracking report for each project above a defined investment threshold.

actions_preview.name: Change request process
actions_preview.desc: Implement a formal change request process to manage scope changes with financial impact.

actions_preview.name: Estimate at completion review
actions_preview.desc: Formally update the estimate at completion (EAC) at each milestone and communicate them to the project sponsor.

actions_preview.name: Requirements freeze process
actions_preview.desc: Introduce a requirements freeze process after the definition phase, with formal change requests for any modifications.

actions_preview.name: Initial stakeholder alignment
actions_preview.desc: Allocate more time to the definition phase to ensure stakeholder buy-in before commencement.

actions_preview.name: Lessons learned on changes
actions_preview.desc: Analyse changes to objectives from recent projects to identify patterns and prevent them in planning.

actions_preview.name: Project startup checklist
actions_preview.desc: Define a standardized project kick-off checklist (team, tools, kickoff, plan) to reduce setup times.

actions_preview.name: Pre-approved resource pool
actions_preview.desc: Proactively define an internal resource pool available for projects, reducing staffing times.

actions_preview.name: Fast-track for urgent projects
actions_preview.desc: Define a fast-tracked procedure for the commencement of high-priority strategic projects.

actions_preview.name: MVP approach
actions_preview.desc: Introduce the practice of defining an MVP (Minimum Viable Product) for each initiative, with the goal of achieving a first result in 60-90 days.

actions_preview.name: Sprint-based delivery
actions_preview.desc: Adopt an iterative approach (2-4 week sprints) with verifiable interim deliverables, even for non-IT projects.

actions_preview.name: Elimination of launch bottlenecks
actions_preview.desc: Identify and remove the main organisational obstacles that slow down the transition from project to operational phase.

blocks.text: When I look at how projects are executed in PMIs, I always see the same pattern, regardless of the project. Deadlines slip, timelines stretch, initial objectives dilute.

What is interesting is that there is rarely a technical issue behind it: there is a web of unspoken issues. Employees do not report risks they see first out of fear they will be perceived as critical. Suppliers do not communicate all the issues to avoid highlighting weaknesses in the newly launched product. Customers do not share backroom details to avoid being exposed. The result is a project proceeding on partial information.

Another deficiency, almost always present: there is no measured starting point. Without it, judgments about the project remain impressionistic. We think things are going well because we hear them or poorly because something doesn’t seem right. The margin of error is enormous and discovery comes too late.

It all starts with clarity of direction: where do we want to go, what transformation do we wish to implement, what results do we aim for. When this is clear to everyone, each person understands their role. Without it, the project operates in a 'they told me to do it that way' mode.

The second point is supplier selection. The right supplier is not the most technically skilled: it’s the one closest to the customer’s way of thinking, the one who understands before they speak. Trust is not a soft factor in the project; it determines whether issues will emerge on time or explode at the end.

No methodology replaces transparency and an outlook that extends beyond the next quarter. PMIs that understand this first generate projects that create value. Others continue to wonder why each project resembles the last.

questions.title: Process automation
questions.text: Data moves from one system to the next automatically, with nothing keyed in twice.
questions.anchor_high: Systems connected, nothing keyed in twice

kpis.name: % of automated vs manual processes
kpis.desc: Percentage of processes executed automatically compared to the total number of processes.

kpis.name: Time saved through automation
kpis.desc: Working time saved once automation is introduced into a process.

kpis.name: % system integration (end-to-end digital)
kpis.desc: Percentage of processes that are fully digital and require no manual intervention between systems.

kpis.name: Number of repetitive manual activities
kpis.desc: Number of repetitive manual activities still being performed that could be automated.

kpis.name: Number of digitised workflows
kpis.desc: Number of workflows that have been digitised and structured within systems.

kpis.name: Number of manual interventions per digital process
kpis.desc: The average number of times an operator must manually intervene in a theoretically digital process.

actions_preview.name: Automation opportunity assessment
actions_preview.desc: Identify and prioritise the processes with the greatest potential for automation (high volume, clear rules, low variability).

actions_preview.name: Quick automation wins
actions_preview.desc: Implement quick automations on the simpler processes (notifications, reports, data transfer) using no-code/low-code tools.

actions_preview.name: Automation roadmap
actions_preview.desc: Define a 12-month automation roadmap with KPIs for tracking and expected ROI for each initiative.

actions_preview.name: Pre-automation baseline
actions_preview.desc: Measure how much manual time each process takes before automating it, so that the benefit can be quantified.

actions_preview.name: Post-implementation review
actions_preview.desc: Conduct a 90-day post-implementation review of each automation, measuring the actual time saved.

actions_preview.name: Reinvestment of freed-up time
actions_preview.desc: Explicitly define how the time saved by automation is reinvested in higher-value activities.

actions_preview.name: Integration landscape mapping
actions_preview.desc: Map all active systems and existing integrations, identifying gaps and points of disconnection.

actions_preview.name: API integration plan
actions_preview.desc: Define a prioritised API integration plan for the most critical systems, starting with processes with the highest number of manual data transfer steps.

actions_preview.name: Integration monitoring
actions_preview.desc: Implement real-time monitoring of existing integrations to detect disruptions and anomalies promptly.

actions_preview.name: Manual activity census
actions_preview.desc: Quantify the repetitive manual activities performed by teams, estimating the weekly time dedicated to each one.

actions_preview.name: RPA quick wins
actions_preview.desc: Implement RPA (Robotic Process Automation) solutions or macros for the most time-consuming repetitive tasks.

actions_preview.name: No-code automation training
actions_preview.desc: Train operational teams on no-code tools (Zapier, Power Automate) to enable them to autonomously automate their activities.

actions_preview.name: Workflow priority mapping
actions_preview.desc: Identify the 10 most critical workflows still managed via email/paper/phone and prioritise them for digitalisation.

actions_preview.name: BPM tool implementation
actions_preview.desc: Implement a workflow management tool (even simple like Microsoft Power Automate or Kissflow) for prioritised workflows.

actions_preview.name: Digital workflow adoption program
actions_preview.desc: Structure a digital workflow adoption program with training, support, and monitoring of usage.

actions_preview.name: Exception analysis
actions_preview.desc: Analyse the causes of major manual interventions in digital processes: unmet rules, missing data, special cases.

actions_preview.name: Rule engine extension
actions_preview.desc: Extend digital process rules to cover more frequent exceptions, reducing manual interventions.

actions_preview.name: Exception SLA
actions_preview.desc: Define Service Level Agreements (SLAs) for managing residual exceptions, assigning ownership and resolution times.

blocks.text: There is one gesture I see in almost every company I walk into, someone reading a number off one screen and typing it into another. Sometimes it’s an order, sometimes an invoice, sometimes a customer record. That gesture is the most visible symptom of two systems that don’t talk to each other.

The national picture confirms this: 49.5% of Italian companies of at least ten employees run an ERP system, but only 21.7% use CRM. Among SMEs, CRM usage drops to 21.1%, compared to 56.5% for large enterprises. The missing piece is usually the one covering the customer.

The reason manual re-keying is so rarely eliminated has little to do with technology. Integrating two systems forces you to decide which of them owns the data, and that decision shifts the balance of power between departments. It is an organisational problem dressed up as a technical one.
Automation starts with mapping rather than with software, because automating chaos simply gives you faster chaos, and the process has to be described before any of it can be automated.

The criterion I use to choose what to automate first is how often the task goes wrong, more than how much time it eats. A repetitive manual task costs you more than the hours it takes, because it also costs you the mistakes that slip through and the time spent putting them right.

One warning I repeat constantly is that automating a broken process makes it permanent. Get the process right first and automate it afterwards, because doing it the other way round carves a way of working into software before anyone has validated it.

references: Istat, 'Firms and ICT, 2025', Statistical Report, 15 December 2025. https://www.istat.it

blocks.text: The quickest test I can do when entering a company is to ask the same number to two different functions. Last month’s revenue, active customers, late deliveries. If the numbers don’t match, and they almost never do, the problem isn’t the data: it’s that no one has decided which is the correct one.

Among Italian SMEs that evaluated an investment in artificial intelligence but did not proceed with it, 45.2% were deterred by the unavailability or poor quality of necessary data. Not due to costs or technology: it was because they lacked the foundational material.

What makes this problem challenging is that it doesn't belong to anyone. Data quality isn't a function's responsibility, so no one owns it, and it continues to deteriorate until someone takes charge of it explicitly.
Governing data means deciding, for every piece of information that matters, who creates it, who corrects it, and what the good version is.

The signal that things are working is simple and immediate: meetings no longer start with a discussion on numbers. When the first quarter hour doesn't need to be spent determining which file is up-to-date, you've gained both time and decision-making clarity.
It's worth stating without equivocation: anything built on poor data inherits the error and amplifies it. A dashboard, an automation, or an AI model. None of these corrects the initial data.

references: Istat, "Imprese e ICT, anno 2025", Statistiche report, 15 dicembre 2025. https://www.istat.it

blocks.text: There are two attitudes towards security, and neither is sustainable. The first hands the whole matter to the supplier, on the grounds that whoever sold the systems will look after them. The second assumes the company is too small to be worth attacking, on the grounds that there is nothing here worth stealing.

The numbers tell a different story. In 2025, Italy recorded 507 serious incidents compared to 357 the previous year, a rise of 42%. Italy alone accounts for 9.6% of the serious attacks detected worldwide, first in Europe and fourth in the world.

Another refrain I hear constantly is that security belongs to the IT department, which it does not. The day the systems go down, the questions coming at you are what data you hold, how long it takes to get back up, and what you tell your customers. Those are questions for whoever runs the company.

I am not an expert in offensive security, and it is not necessary to be one. What is needed comes first and is almost always missing, namely knowing what has to be protected, what it is worth and what happens if it stops working.

From that foundation, everything else follows, ordered by importance rather than by the supplier's catalogue. The same money spent on a plan is worth far more than the same money spent piece by piece on individual products.
The factor that decides everything is testing, because an untested plan is not a plan. Finding out that the backups do not restore should never happen on the day you need them.

references: Clusit, "CLUSIT 2026 ICT Security Report", March 2026. https://clusit.it/rapporto-clusit/

blocks.text: The moment I realize that an instrument has not been adopted is when I ask to see the actual file being worked on. There is almost always one, and it is a spreadsheet that lives alongside the paid software costing tens of thousands of euros.

The gap between those who adopt and those who lag behind is widening, not closing: on artificial intelligence, the distance between PMIs and large enterprises has increased from twenty points in 2023 to twenty-five in 2024, up to thirty-seven by 2025.

The change resistance I most frequently encounter is not about the reluctance to change. It's that the tool was chosen based on a feature list rather than actual work requirements, and the person who would use it saw it for the first time on the day of the training.
Unadopted software is not a neutral cost. It continues to incur expenses, with more work done outside the system leading to more data that do not reach where they are needed.

The right question before purchasing is not which product is better. It's who will use it every day and what it simplifies for them. If there isn't an answer to this second part, adoption won't happen, no matter how good the product is.

Before buying something new, I would check what we already have. In my experience, a significant portion of what we need was purchased years ago and is not being used simply because nobody has ever explained that it exists.

references: Istat, 'Firms and ICT, 2025', Statistical Report, 15 December 2025. https://www.istat.it

blocks.text: The phrase I hear most often when a project stalls is that there's a lack of time. When I dig deeper, the issue isn't really about time: it's a lack of someone who knows how to do that task, and no one wants to say it out loud.

National data confirms this clearly: among Italian companies that evaluated an investment in artificial intelligence but then did not proceed, almost 60% stopped due to a lack of adequate skills. Not because of the technology cost: because no one knew who would make it work.

The point that interests me is different: the missing competence is rarely technical. It is governance competence, i.e., knowing how to define what you want, choosing a supplier, and ensuring that what arrives is what was needed.
Mapping competencies is not about distributing grades. It is about understanding which decisions the company can make on its own and which ones it cannot.

On this, I have a conviction drawn from construction sites: competencies are not acquired solely by hiring. A significant part of them is built by supporting existing people, which costs less and lasts longer.

The criterion for deciding what to keep in-house and what to outsource is simple: anything that is central to your competitive advantage must be something you can do yourself. The rest can be outsourced, provided it can be properly evaluated.

references: Istat, 'Firms and ICT, 2025', Statistical Report, 15 December 2025. https://www.istat.it

blocks.text: When I enter a company, I always ask my colleagues one question: what would you change if you could. The responses are almost always precise, concrete, and well-thought-out. This means that the ideas exist, but they have never been asked for.
When a proposal from below is ignored twice, the third does not come. Not out of spite: for economy. People stop spending energy where they have learned that it produces no effect.

The connection with the rest is direct. If nobody knows the direction, nobody can propose something that goes in that direction. Initiative is not a matter of character; it is a consequence of the context people have.
Engagement is not achieved by communicating more. It is achieved by showing that something has changed because someone said so.
In the yards where I worked, the first sign that transformation was taking root was never an indicator. It was that in meetings, people who used to be silent started speaking.

There remains a responsibility that cannot be delegated: individuals do not take ownership of outcomes they did not help define. Asking for ownership over top-down set objectives is asking for something that does not exist.

blocks.text: Training is the expense item that I find easier to justify and verify. A course is purchased, a classroom is filled, and a certificate is archived. Whether something has changed in daily work practices, no one checks that.

The breaking point is not in the classroom but upon returning to the desk. The individual returns, finds the same tools and deadlines as before, and within a week, they revert to their previous habits.

When I ask a manager what they expect to see different after the course, the response is almost always generic. If those sending people for training cannot specify what should change, they won't be able to notice if it has changed.
Training works when those returning to work have the permission and opportunity to use what they have learned. Without that opportunity, within a few weeks, the investment will have evaporated.
For this reason, what matters is not the classroom; it's the three months following: support, a real case to apply it to, someone to ask when you get stuck.
The quickest way to understand if training has worked is not through an end-of-course test. It’s about looking, three months later, to see if a task is being performed differently from before.

Manifattura e produzione.testo: In your sector, 45.9% of companies analyse their data and 59.9% use an ERP management system. CRM adoption is at 19.0%; manufacturing has a good understanding of its production but much less about its customers.

Commercio e distribuzione.testo: Your sector leads Italy in CRM adoption with 29.9%, and 52.5% of companies analyse their data. However, only 19.1% derive at least 1% of revenue from online sales.

Servizi alle imprese.testo: Among professional and technical activities, 46.2% analyse data and 56.9% use an ERP. In rental and business support services, these figures drop to 42.5% and 38.5%, respectively.

Servizi alle persone.testo: The accommodation and food service industries have the lowest values in Italy alongside construction: 32.4% on data analysis, 28.5% on management. However, 34.6% sell online, which is the highest figure across all sectors.

Costruzioni e immobiliare.testo: Construction is the least digitised sector in Italy: with only 28.4% on data analysis compared to an average of 42.7%, and CRM at just 11.3%. The real estate sector performs better, at 48.7%, but still lags behind with a CRM rate of 17.7%.

Agricoltura, energia e risorse.testo: More than 40% of agricultural businesses use at least one 4.0 solution, but over half are behind on digitalisation, with the most common challenges being absent interoperability and limited skills. In energy provision, the picture is reversed: 53.6% on data analysis and 43.7% on CRM, among the highest in Italy.
Agricoltura, energia e risorse.fonte: Istat, Enterprises and ICT, December 2025 · Smart AgriFood Observatory, Politecnico di Milano, February 2025

Altro / Multi-settore.testo: In Italy, 42.7% of companies with at least ten employees analyse their own data. While 79.5% of SMEs have a basic level of digitalisation, only 37.3% reach an advanced level.
